text: What year were the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations introduced?
explanation: The Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR) were introduced in 2003, implementing an EU directive on privacy in electronic communications.

text: What are the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations commonly known as?

options.text: GDPR
PECR
RIPA
PIPEDA

explanation: The Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations are commonly abbreviated to PECR — they sit alongside GDPR and are enforced by the Information Commissioner's Office.

text: What is the primary focus of PECR?

options.text: Regulating the physical disposal of electronic devices
Protecting privacy in electronic communications — covering cookies, marketing calls, texts and emails
Setting standards for broadband infrastructure
Controlling surveillance by public bodies

explanation: PECR focuses on protecting privacy in electronic communications — covering cookies, direct marketing via calls, texts and emails, and the confidentiality of communications.

text: What do PECR rules on cookies require?

options.text: All cookies must be encrypted
Websites must tell users about cookies, explain what they do and obtain consent before placing non-essential cookies
Cookies can only be used for 24 hours
All cookies must be deleted after each browsing session

explanation: Under PECR, websites must inform users about cookies, explain what they do, and get consent before placing non-essential cookies — this is why websites show cookie consent banners.

text: What is an example of a cookie that is exempt from PECR consent requirements?

options.text: Advertising and tracking cookies
Strictly necessary cookies — such as those that keep items in a shopping basket
Analytics cookies that track user behaviour
Social media sharing cookies

explanation: Strictly necessary cookies — such as those needed to keep items in a shopping basket or maintain a login session — are exempt from PECR consent requirements as they are essential to the service.

text: What does PECR say about unsolicited direct marketing by email?

options.text: It is allowed without restriction
You must have prior consent from the recipient before sending marketing emails to individuals
Marketing emails are only allowed on weekdays
Only charities are exempt from the rules

explanation: PECR requires prior consent before sending marketing emails to individuals — this is why legitimate marketing emails include an unsubscribe option and require opt-in consent.

text: What is the 'soft opt-in' rule under PECR?

options.text: A relaxed consent rule allowing marketing to anyone who has ever visited your website
An exception allowing marketing to existing customers about similar products if they were given a chance to opt out when their details were collected
A rule that only applies to SMS marketing
Permission to email anyone who has not actively objected

explanation: The soft opt-in allows businesses to market similar products or services to existing customers without explicit consent, provided the customer was given an easy opt-out when their details were first collected.

text: Which organisation enforces PECR in the UK?

options.text: The Health and Safety Executive
The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)
Ofcom
The Environment Agency

explanation: The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) enforces PECR alongside GDPR — it can issue fines to organisations that breach the regulations.

text: What are nuisance calls and how does PECR address them?

options.text: Nuisance calls are legal and PECR does not restrict them
PECR restricts unsolicited marketing calls — people can register with the Telephone Preference Service to opt out
PECR only covers email marketing, not phone calls
All marketing calls require a court order

explanation: PECR restricts unsolicited direct marketing calls. Individuals can register with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) to opt out, and companies must screen against the TPS before calling.

text: How does PECR relate to GDPR?

options.text: PECR replaced GDPR in the UK
PECR sits alongside GDPR — GDPR covers personal data broadly while PECR adds specific rules for electronic communications and marketing
GDPR overrides PECR in all cases
They cover completely different areas with no overlap

explanation: PECR sits alongside GDPR — GDPR provides broad data protection rules while PECR adds specific requirements for cookies, electronic marketing and the confidentiality of communications.

text: A company wants to send a promotional text message to a list of mobile numbers they purchased. What does PECR require?

options.text: Nothing — purchased data lists can be freely used for marketing
The recipients must have given prior consent to receive marketing messages from this type of company
They must send one free product before any marketing message
They must register the list with the ICO

explanation: Under PECR, recipients must have given prior consent to receive marketing texts. Simply purchasing a list does not give the right to send unsolicited marketing messages.

text: What must a website do when a user first visits, under PECR cookie rules?

options.text: Block all cookies automatically until the user logs in
Inform the user about non-essential cookies and obtain their consent before setting them
Display a full list of all cookies used in the footer
Email the user a summary of cookies used

explanation: Websites must inform users about non-essential cookies and obtain clear consent before setting them — this is why cookie consent banners are required on almost every website.

text: What is the maximum fine the ICO can issue for serious PECR breaches?

options.text: £17.5 million or 4% of global turnover
There is no maximum fine

explanation: Following the UK GDPR alignment, the ICO can issue fines of up to £17.5 million or 4% of global annual turnover for the most serious PECR breaches.

text: What does PECR say about the confidentiality of communications?

options.text: All electronic communications can be monitored by service providers
Communications must be kept confidential — service providers must not intercept or monitor them without lawful authority
Confidentiality only applies to phone calls, not emails
Confidentiality rules only apply to government communications

explanation: PECR requires that communications are kept confidential — service providers must not listen to, store or monitor communications without lawful authority or the user's consent.

text: Which EU directive did PECR implement into UK law?

options.text: The EU WEEE Directive
The EU ePrivacy Directive
The EU Product Liability Directive
The EU Digital Single Market Directive

explanation: PECR implemented the EU ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC) into UK law, which updated rules on privacy in electronic communications to cover the internet age.
